property_management.structure_note: Property management shares its licensing foundation with real_estate_brokerage.json -- both are regulated as brokerage activity under Tex. Occ. Code Section 1101.002 (TRELA), and a property management company controlling rent collection or leasing for a third-party owner generally must hold or operate under a TREC broker license, same as a sales brokerage. CONFIRMED 2026-08-30: the narrow exemptions (on-site apartment managers with an office at the property, employees of an owner managing only that owner's property) do NOT cover third-party professional property management companies collecting management fees -- do not assume a property management client is exempt without checking which category they actually fall into. What genuinely distinguishes this industry from real_estate_brokerage is the ONGOING landlord-tenant relationship layer under Tex. Prop. Code Chapter 92 (security deposits, habitability, eviction procedure) -- a pure sales-focused brokerage never touches this; a property manager deals with it on every tenancy.

Business Entity Broker License (TREC): Tex. Occ. Code Section 1101.002 (TRELA) -- controlling the acceptance or deposit of rent, leasing units, negotiating lease terms, or marketing vacancies for another for compensation constitutes real estate brokerage activity requiring licensure. CONFIRMED 2026-08-30 across multiple sources. Exemptions are narrow: on-site apartment managers with an office at the property, and employees of an owner managing only that owner's property. Neither exemption covers a third-party professional property management company.
Notice of Landlord/Property Manager Iden: Tex. Prop. Code Sections 92.201-92.205 (Subchapter E, Disclosure of Ownership and Management) -- requires disclosure of BOTH the landlord's identity and the property manager's identity, a property-management-specific obligation with no direct equivalent in real_estate_brokerage.json.
Security Deposit Itemized Deduction Stat: Tex. Prop. Code Section 92.103 (30-day return of deposit, clock starts when the tenant surrenders the property AND provides a written forwarding address) and Section 92.104 (a written, itemized description of deductions is required -- receipts alone do not satisfy the statute). Section 92.109 creates a bad-faith presumption if the landlord misses the 30-day deadline or fails to provide the written accounting, exposing the landlord/manager to a statutory penalty plus attorney's fees. CONFIRMED 2026-08-30 across multiple independent sources.
Habitability / Repair Request Log: Tex. Prop. Code Sections 92.051-92.062 (Subchapter B) -- the landlord's duty to repair conditions materially affecting a tenant's health or safety, tenant notice requirements, and tenant remedies including repair-and-deduct (Section 92.0561) and judicial remedies (Section 92.0563).
Smoke Alarm Compliance Records: Tex. Prop. Code Sections 92.251-92.262 (Subchapter F) -- required smoke detectors, replacement batteries, and tenant remedies for landlord noncompliance.
Security Device Compliance Records (lock: Tex. Prop. Code Sections 92.151-92.170 (Subchapter D) -- required locks, peepholes, latches, door viewers, window security, and tenant rekeying rights.
Lockout Compliance Documentation: Tex. Prop. Code Section 92.0081 -- prohibits a landlord from removing doors, windows, hardware, or furniture, or excluding a tenant from the premises, except by judicial process. Narrow carveouts exist for bona fide repair/replacement, tenant abandonment, and a specifically-defined rent-delinquency lockout procedure with strict written notice and locksmith-coordination requirements. 'Self-help' eviction outside these carveouts is one of the most expensive mistakes a Texas landlord or property manager can make.
Notice to Vacate: Tex. Prop. Code Chapter 24 (forcible detainer) -- the judicial eviction process. A notice to vacate (commonly a minimum of 3 days unless the lease states otherwise) must precede filing, followed by a Justice of the Peace court filing, hearing, and writ of possession. No self-help eviction is permitted.
Anti-Retaliation Compliance Checklist: Tex. Prop. Code Sections 92.331-92.335 -- creates a 6-month window after a tenant's protected action (such as requesting a repair) during which specified landlord actions (filing eviction, decreasing services, certain rent increases) are presumed retaliatory.
